name: Nasturtium herb with horseradish root (combination tablets)
short: Rats only: fetal and kidney harm (nasturtium), bladder tumour promotion (horseradish). People, with horseradish: no significant adverse-effect difference in 1 trial; 36 vs 37 on placebo in another.
text: All the human data are for nasturtium herb (Tropaeolum majus) combined with horseradish root, taken by mouth; no human data on nasturtium alone were found. Trials: in a phase III trial in 217 women with recurrent cystitis who took the combination (110) or placebo (107) for 6 months, there were no significant differences between groups in any reported adverse effect. In an earlier 90-day placebo-controlled trial (174 patients enrolled), 36 patients on the combination and 37 on placebo reported adverse events; two serious adverse events occurred with placebo and one with the combination, which was not associated with the study medication. In a placebo-controlled trial of respiratory-infection prevention in 351 adults (up to 84 days), adverse events were recorded and the authors describe the product as well tolerated, and in a trial against the antibiotic co-trimoxazole in 96 patients with acute cystitis both treatments were well tolerated; neither abstract gives numbers. Observational studies: adverse events were recorded in 1.5% of 1,223 patients aged 4 and over taking the combination and 6.8% of 426 given standard antibiotics; in 0.6% of 523 children and adolescents taking it and 3.9% of 335 given antibiotics; and, in 96 inpatients with catheter-associated urinary infection, adverse events and adverse drug reactions occurred in 23.8% of those taking the combination alone, 44.8% of those taking it with antibiotics and 34.5% of those taking antibiotics alone. These groups were not randomised. Pregnancy (animal data only): in pregnant rats, a Tropaeolum majus extract at high doses lowered ACE activity and aldosterone and was linked to fetal growth retardation and kidney damage, which the authors relate to ACE-inhibitor-like activity. Horseradish extract (rat data only): given in drinking water, it caused overgrowth of the bladder lining and, after a chemical carcinogen, promoted bladder papillomas and carcinomas, although a 104-week study found no treatment-related increase in tumours. No human data on these effects and no interaction data were found in the cited sources.
